extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for filing and evaluating petitions to revive U.S. patent applications (37 CFR 1.137), including what constitutes the required reply, fee and evidence requirements, and standards for "unintentional" versus "unavoidable" delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required reply (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the required reply is the reply sufficient to have avoided abandonment, had such reply been timely filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition for an extension of time under 37 CFR 1.136 and a fee for such an extension of time are not required to be included with the reply. The specific form of the required reply depends on the reason for abandonment (e.g., failure to pay fees, failure to reply to Office action, failure to file appeal brief, failure to notify foreign filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue fee / publication fee requirement for revival
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application or patent is abandoned or lapsed for failure to pay the issue fee or any portion thereof, the required reply must include payment of the issue fee or any outstanding balance; if abandoned for failure to pay the publication fee, the required reply must include payment of the publication fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice of Allowance requires timely payment of the issue fee in effect on the date of mailing to avoid abandonment. If issue fee increases, Office will mail notice requiring payment of the balance. Filing a continuing application without payment of the issue fee or outstanding balance is not an acceptable reply for abandonment due to failure to pay the issue fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable replies for abandonment for failure to reply to a non-final action
rubrics_metrics.description: The required reply may be either (A) an argument or an amendment under 37 CFR 1.111, or (B) the filing of a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or a CPA under 37 CFR 1.53(d) for design applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The grant of a petition under 37 CFR 1.137 is not a determination that any reply under 37 CFR 1.111 is complete; petitions may be granted if the reply 'appears to be bona fide', but examiners may later require corrections under a shortened statutory period (1 month under 37 CFR 1.135(c)). Extensions of time under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are permitted for such corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required reply for abandonment for failure to reply to a final action
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply under 37 CFR 1.113 to a final action must include a request for continued examination (RCE) under 37 CFR 1.114 or cancellation of, or appeal from the rejection of, each claim so rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable replies for a nonprovisional abandoned for failure to reply to a final action include: (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE (with a submission that meets 37 CFR 1.111 and the requisite fee) under 37 CFR 1.114 for utility/plant applications filed on or after June 8, 1995; or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for design).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a proposed amendment is routed for allowance determination
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 is filed as the required reply, the Office will normally route the amendment to the Technology Center to determine whether it places the application in condition for allowance before granting any petition to revive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner indicates the reply places the application in condition for allowance, examiner should mark 'OK to enter upon revival' and petition will be granted if otherwise grantable. If not, examiner completes PTOL-303 and returns to Office of Petitions; Office will not grant the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable replies for abandonment for failure to file an appeal brief
rubrics_metrics.description: When abandonment occurred due to failure to file an appeal brief, the reply required pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) or 1.137(b)(1) must be either: (A) an appeal brief in compliance with 37 CFR 41.37(c) and appeal brief fee; (B) the filing of an RCE accompanied by a submission and the requisite fee in compliance with 37 CFR 1.114 (for qualifying applications); or (C) the filing of a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) for design applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a notice of appeal is the reply, the time period under 37 CFR 41.37 for filing the appeal brief will be set by the Director in the petition decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing an RCE as the required reply: responsiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When an RCE is filed as the reply to revive (for failure to reply to a final Office action or failure to file an appeal brief), the submission accompanying the RCE must be a reply responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111 to the last Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration of responsiveness is done without factoring in the 'final' status of the action. The submission may be a previously filed amendment after final or a statement that incorporates by reference arguments in a previously filed appeal or reply brief. Petition may be granted if submission 'appears to be a bona fide attempt' to provide a complete reply; examiners may later require corrections under a 1-month shortened statutory period (37 CFR 1.135(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office may require continuing application or RCE where reply would impose inordinate burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may require filing of a continuing application or an RCE to meet the reply requirement where treating a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113 would place an inordinate burden on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary circumstances include: (A) an application abandoned for an inordinate period of time; (B) application file contains multiple or conflicting replies to the last Office action; (C) the reply or replies submitted under 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) (or (b)(1)) are questionable as to compliance with 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpublication request + foreign filing notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant makes a nonpublication request and subsequently files a counterpart application in a foreign country (or PCT route) that requires eighteen-month publication, the nonpublication request must be rescinded and the Office notified of the foreign filing within forty-five days after the date of such filing; failure to provide timely notice results in abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revival for abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 122(b)(2)(B)(iii) is only on the basis of 'unintentional' delay (37 CFR 1.137(b)). The reply requirement of 37 CFR 1.137(c) is met by the notification of such foreign filing. A petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) to revive will not stay any running periods against the application. Applicants may use form PTO/SB/64a for such petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee requirement and fee rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revival of an unintentionally abandoned application or for unintentional delayed payment of the issue fee must be accompanied by the petition fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m), unless the petition is filed under 35 U.S.C. 133 or 151 (on the basis of unavoidable delay), in which case the fee is set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase '[o]n filing' means the petition fee is required on filing the petition (not merely on grant). The Office will not refund the petition fee required by 37 CFR 1.17(l) or 1.17(m) regardless of whether the petition is dismissed or denied, and will not reach the merits of any petition lacking the requisite fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unintentional vs unavoidable delay distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are evaluated under the 'unintentional delay' standard (less stringent) while petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(a) require a showing of 'unavoidable' delay (more exacting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unavoidable delay is the epitome of unintentional delay. A petition under 1.137(a) must establish unavoidable (not merely unintentional) delay, and thus requires more documentary evidence and is less likely to be grantable as filed than petitions under 1.137(b). Many petitions filed under 1.137(a) end up granted under 1.137(b) when adequate evidence of unavoidable delay is not obtainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unintentional delay: acceptable statement and duty of candor
rubrics_metrics.description: For a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b), the Office generally accepts a statement that 'the entire delay ... was unintentional' based on the applicant's or practitioner's duty of candor (37 CFR 10.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office relies on the applicant's duty of candor and good faith and accepts the unintentional statement without requiring further information in the vast majority of petitions under 1.137(b). However, providing an inappropriate statement may have adverse effects (e.g., inequitable conduct) when enforcing resulting patents; applicants are advised to include the unintentional-delay statement and may use PTO/SB/64, PTO/SB/64a, or PTO/SB/64PCT forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentional/deliberate abandonment precludes 'unintentional' finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action on the part of the applicant (e.g., concluding claims are unpatentable, deferring prosecution/fees, deciding patent has insufficient value) is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of deliberate courses of action that preclude unintentional delay include: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable over references; (B) applicant does not consider allowed/patentable claims of sufficient breadth to justify expense; (C) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to justify expense; (D) applicant does not consider any patent of sufficient value to maintain interest; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and prosecution expenses. A subsequent change of mind does not convert a prior deliberate decision into 'unintentional.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence needed to show 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of unavoidable delay (for petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(a)) requires evidence concerning: (1) procedures in place that should have avoided the error resulting in the delay; (2) training and experience of persons responsible for the error; and (3) copies of any applicable docketing records to show the error was the cause of the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 1.137(a) requires unavoidable delay (a higher standard), the petition must establish that the entire delay from due date for the reply until filing of a grantable petition was unavoidable. Applicants often find obtaining sufficient evidence difficult, which is why many petitions convert to 1.137(b) filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably prudent person standard for 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions on reviving abandoned applications on the basis of 'unavoidable' delay adopt the reasonably prudent person standard: 'requires no more or greater care or diligence than is generally used and observed by prudent and careful men in relation to their most important business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard permits reliance upon ordinary agencies of mail and telegraph, trustworthy employees, and usual instrumentalities; if failure occurred unexpectedly or through unforeseen faults of such agencies, and all other conditions of promptness exist, delay may be 'unavoidable.' Decisions are made case-by-case taking all facts and circumstances into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical error as basis for unavoidable delay (three-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a clerical error by an employee may support a showing of 'unavoidable' delay provided it is shown that: (A) the error was the cause of the delay; (B) there was a business routine in place for performing the clerical function that could reasonably be relied upon to avoid errors; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained and experienced that reliance upon them represented due care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include In re Egbers and In re Katrapat. Exemplary application: change of correspondence address causing mailing to old address—adequate showing of unavoidable delay requires proof of due care to notify Office promptly and in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does NOT constitute 'unavoidable' delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay resulting from lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice or the MPEP, or failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8 or 1.10, does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: permitting the maximum extendable statutory period for reply to a final Office action to expire while awaiting allowance; relying on oral advice from USPTO employees; USPTO's failure to advise does not render applicant's delay unavoidable. See Haines v. Quigg, Vincent v. Mossinghoff, Smith v. Diamond, Potter v. Dann, Ex parte Murray, In re Sivertz.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper notification of change of correspondence address
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely and adequate notification of a change in correspondence address is required to preserve timely receipt of Office mail; certain practices do not constitute proper notification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improper notifications include: (A) mere inclusion of a different address in a paper filed for another purpose without mention that an address change is being made; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as affected (except as provided under Customer Number practice - MPEP § 403); (C) lack of notification or belated notification to the USPTO of the change in correspondence address. Adequate showing of unavoidable delay for an address-related loss requires evidence of timely notification made in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods considered in evaluation of petitions (three periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three periods to consider during evaluation of a petition under 37 CFR 1.137: (A) the delay in reply that originally resulted in the abandonment; (B) the delay in filing an initial petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137 to revive the application; and (C) the delay in filing a grantable petition pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137 to revive the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For unavoidable-delay petitions under 1.137(a), the petitioner must show that the entire delay across these periods was unavoidable; failure to file a petition 'promptly' upon becoming aware of abandonment undermines a showing of unavoidable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural consequences and practical guidance on petition type selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Because petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(a) (unavoidable delay) are more exacting, applicants should consider filing under 1.137(b) (unintentional) when evidence of unavoidable delay is difficult to obtain; petitions under 1.137(a) often generate interlocutory requests for more evidence and take longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office will often grant petitions under 1.137(b) based on statements and minimal documentation. A petition under 1.137(a) must include sufficient showing that the entire delay was unavoidable; if not, it may be denied or dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-refundability and filing-timing of petition fee
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition fee required by 37 CFR 1.17(l) or 1.17(m) is due on filing the petition and will not be refunded regardless of the petition outcome; the Office will not reach merits for petitions lacking the requisite fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implements congressional direction that fees are due on filing. The phrase '[o]n filing' is interpreted literally by the Office.
